title: What are the areas of squares with these three sides?
description: The video finds the area of squares whose sides are a whole number, a fraction and a decimal, by multiplying the side by itself, and names the perfect square among them. Keeko doubts the area after adding the side to itself.
teaching_notes: One idea: the area of a square is its side multiplied by itself, whatever kind of number the side is. A perfect square needs a natural number side. Watch for students who add the side twice instead of multiplying.

source: Find the areas of squares with sides 6 units, 3/5 unit and 2.5 units.
video_script.why: The child sees that the area of a square is side times side for every kind of side, and that only a natural number side gives a perfect square.
video_script.substitution: Multiply the side by itself, then check if the side is a natural number.
video_script.anchor: three squares drawn with sides six units, three fifths of a unit and two point five units
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko adds six and six to get twelve square units. Twelve unit squares fill only two of the six rows, so the side must be multiplied by itself.
video_script.payoff_line: The areas are thirty six, nine twenty fifths and six point two five square units

final_answer.spoken: thirty six, nine twenty fifths and six point two five square units

never_show: the side lengths of the exercise videos of the topic
maths_rules: area of a square = side × side = side²
perfect squares are the squares of natural numbers: 36 = 6² is one; 9/25 and 6.25 are not, because 3/5 and 2.5 are not natural numbers
the slip: 6 + 6 = 12 adds the side to itself, and 12 unit squares fill only 2 of the 6 rows
video_script.design: One idea: area of a square is side times side. Wrong idea: adding the side twice. The three squares stay in the anchor band.

beats.on_screen: a small title card From your book; three squares in the anchor band, labelled with sides 6 units, 3/5 unit and 2.5 units, each with an empty area box

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This question is from your book.
<bookmark mark='squares'/>Three squares have sides six units, three fifths of a unit and two point five units.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>What is the area of each square?

beats.on_screen: the question holds still and the three empty area boxes glow

marks.stop: the three empty boxes glow in the accent colour

narration: <bookmark mark='stop'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: a square of side 4 units cut into 4 rows of 4 unit squares; the line area = side × side appears

marks.grid: a square of side four is cut into unit squares
marks.rows: the four rows of four unit squares are counted
marks.rule: the line area = side × side appears

narration: <bookmark mark='grid'/>Area counts the unit squares inside a square.
<bookmark mark='rows'/>A square of side four units has four rows, and each row holds four unit squares.
<bookmark mark='rule'/>Its area is four times four, the side times the side.
<bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the sides are six units, three fifths of a unit and two point five units.

beats.on_screen: To find: the area of each square

marks.find: the thing to find is written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the area of each square.
<bookmark mark='six'/>Step one, multiply the side by itself. Six times six is thirty six square units.
We write six times six as six squared.

marks.top: 3 × 3 is written over the fraction bar
marks.bottom: 5 × 5 is written under the bar and the fraction 9/25 appears

narration: <bookmark mark='top'/>Step two, multiply three fifths by three fifths. Three times three is nine on top.
<bookmark mark='bottom'/>Five times five is twenty five at the bottom, so the area is nine twenty fifths.
<bookmark mark='dec'/>Step three, multiply two point five by two point five.
That gives six point two five square units.

beats.on_screen: 36 = 6² is a perfect square; 9/25 and 6.25 are not

marks.nat: the sides 6, 3/5 and 2.5 are compared, and only 6 is ringed
marks.name: the words perfect square appear beside 36

narration: <bookmark mark='nat'/>Step four, only six is a natural number.
<bookmark mark='name'/>The squares of natural numbers are called perfect squares, so thirty six is one.
<bookmark mark='ans'/>The areas are thirty six, nine twenty fifths and six point two five square units.
<bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble: 6 + 6 = 12 square units; two rows of the grid light up and stop short of six rows

marks.short: twelve unit squares fill only two rows of the six-by-six grid
marks.fix: all six rows fill up and the bubble is struck

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks the area of the first square is twelve square units, because six and six make twelve.
<bookmark mark='short'/>Twelve unit squares fill only two rows of this square.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>It has six rows of six, so we multiply the side by itself.
